analysis.one_liner: Bans federal government use of facial recognition and biometric surveillance unless Congress explicitly authorizes it.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered by either committee it was sent to and never received a House vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful for any federal agency, employee, or contractor to acquire or use facial recognition, gait recognition, or voice recognition surveillance systems anywhere in the United States, unless Congress later passes a law that specifically names who may use the technology, for what purposes, and with what accuracy and privacy safeguards. Information obtained through illegal use could not be used as evidence in federal cases, individuals could sue for damages, and state and local governments would lose federal Byrne law enforcement grants unless they adopt similar bans.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who would otherwise be subject to constant, automated government identification in public places, at airports, and at the border. The burden of facial recognition misidentification falls hardest on people of color, women, and older people, so a ban protects them most. It also preserves the ability of anyone to walk or gather in public without the government logging their face, voice, or gait.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People photographed or filmed in public places

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits every federal agency, employee, contractor, and subcontractor from acquiring or using facial recognition, gait recognition, or voice recognition systems in the United States, including airports, ports of entry, and border zones, unless a future act of Congress specifically authorizes it with accuracy audits and due-process protections [S3].

Bars the federal government from using information obtained through unlawful biometric surveillance in any criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding, and gives individuals the right to sue for actual and punitive damages plus attorney's fees [S3].

Cuts off federal Byrne public safety grants to any state or local government that does not adopt a substantially similar prohibition, which pushes the ban down to police departments and city agencies [S2].
Bars federal law enforcement agencies from spending any federal funds, including unallocated funds, on purchasing or using biometric surveillance systems [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies lose a surveillance tool they have increasingly used for investigations, monitoring protests, and identification at borders. Facial recognition and biometric technology companies lose the government market for their products, including both software sales and government contracts. Agencies argue the technology helps solve crimes and identify suspects, and they would bear the cost of losing it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies and surveillance tech firms

drawbacks.text: Law enforcement agencies would lose a tool they use to identify suspects, find missing people, and match faces to evidence; the bill gives agencies no pathway to use the technology even for narrowly limited, audited purposes, because only a future act of Congress can authorize any use [S3].

The grant condition applies to state and local governments, which could cost some police departments federal public safety funding until they change their own laws or policies to match the federal ban [S3].

The bill is a moratorium, not a regulatory framework; it leaves the federal government with no facial recognition capability at all until Congress drafts the detailed authorization the bill requires, a high bar that could take years [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: facial recognition has documented accuracy problems, and mistaken identification can cost an innocent person their liberty, while police agencies see genuine investigative value in the technology. The bill resolves the trade-off by defaulting entirely against government use until Congress authorizes it with specific safeguards — a strong version of the privacy position. Whether that is the right balance depends on how much weight you give to the risk of automated misidentification versus the investigative value to police; the bill clearly weights privacy far heavier.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary and Oversight and Reform committees, which took no further action on it, so it died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on June 15, 2021, joined by seven original cosponsors: Reps. Pressley, Tlaib, Eshoo, Espaillat, Norton, Omar, and Rush [S3].

The bill was referred the same day to the Committee on the Judiciary and, in addition, to the Committee on Oversight and Reform, with consideration of the relevant provisions left to each committee [S5].
Sixteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total [S4].

Neither committee held a markup or brought the bill to the floor; the congressional record shows no further action after the initial referral, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies and biometric surveillance technology vendors, who keep the existing status quo: government use of facial recognition continues without the restrictions or private right of action this bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies and surveillance tech vendors

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all 16 cosponsors were House Democrats, so any support the bill had was entirely one-party, and no opposition is on the record.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance technology vendors
industries.note: These companies sell identification software to federal agencies, police departments, and border authorities; the bill cuts off the government market and lets individuals sue over unlawful use. Their revenue depends on a practice that subjects ordinary people to automated government identification without consent.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement and border agencies
industries.note: Agencies that use facial recognition for investigations, airport screening, and border identification would be barred from acquiring or using the systems and from funding them with any federal dollars. Their investigative interest runs against the privacy interest of the people they surveil.

Departments using facial recognition would have to adopt matching bans to keep Byrne grant money, so they would lose either the technology or the funding. The money at stake is a real share of many local public safety budgets.
